h1: Hazy or clear: what cloudiness tells you about a beer
title: Hazy or Clear Beer: What Haze Means | Craft Beer School
desc: What makes a beer hazy or clear, when cloudiness is intended and when it is a fault, plus how to read the glass before you taste.
teaser: A cloudy IPA is meant to look like orange juice. A cloudy lager is usually telling you something went wrong. Here is how to tell.
standfirst: Haze is one of the first things you notice about a beer and one of the most misunderstood. Some beers should be cloudy, some should be brilliant. A few look wrong for a reason worth knowing.
sections:
Haze is tiny particles suspended in the beer that scatter light. In most beers they come from a few sources:

  • Yeast. Cells still in suspension after fermentation.
  • Protein and polyphenols. Proteins from malt bind with polyphenols from malt husk and hops to form particles.
  • Hop material. Heavy dry hopping leaves fine particles and oils in the beer.
  • Starch. Unconverted starch from an incomplete mash, a sign of a brewing problem.
  • Microbes. Bacteria or wild yeast from an infection.

Our deeper guide to beer haze causes covers the chemistry. For drinking purposes, the question is whether the haze belongs in that style.

Some styles are cloudy by design. A hefeweizen is unfiltered, with yeast in suspension that adds banana and clove. A witbier is pale and cloudy from wheat and oats. A New England IPA is famous for looking like juice, with haze from oats, wheat, heavy dry hopping and yeast that stays in suspension.

In these beers haze is part of the texture as well as the look. It gives a softer, rounder mouthfeel. A hazy IPA that dropped crystal clear would usually mean something unusual had happened to it.

Pilsners, helles, most lagers, pale ales in the British style and many Belgian ales are expected to be clear, sometimes brilliantly so. Brewers get them there with time and cold. Beer held at around 0 to 2 °C for several days lets yeast and protein particles drop to the bottom of the tank. Finings such as isinglass or silica speed this up. Some breweries filter.

A cloudy pilsner is not automatically bad. Some unfiltered lagers are sold proudly that way. But if the menu promises a crisp pils and the glass looks murky, it is fair to ask why.
Chill haze and when to worry

Chill haze is the most common harmless cloudiness. Protein and polyphenol particles form when beer is very cold, then dissolve again as it warms. Hold a hazy-looking lager in your hand for a few minutes. If it clears, it was chill haze. It affects the look, not the flavour.

Indian conditions make chill haze more common than it needs to be. Beer that is warmed and chilled repeatedly on its way through distribution, sitting in a hot godown and then a cold shop fridge, tends to form more stable haze over time. That same cycling also speeds up staling.

Haze that does not clear, combined with odd flavours, is more worrying. A lager that tastes sour, smells of vinegar or has a ropey, oily texture may be infected. A beer that was clear when fresh and has gone cloudy on the shelf is also a warning sign, especially if the flavour has gone flat or stale. Old hazy IPAs can turn murky brown in colour as their hop compounds oxidise.
Reading the glass before you sip

Hold the glass against the light and look through it. Ask three questions.

  1. Is this a style that should be clear or hazy?
  2. Is the haze even, or are there floating flecks and sediment?
  3. Does the colour look fresh, or dull and brownish?

Even haze in an NEIPA is fine. Large floating clumps in a bottle may be yeast sediment, which is harmless and often deliberate in bottle-conditioned beers. Pour gently and leave the last centimetre in the bottle if you want a clearer glass. With a hefeweizen, the tradition runs the other way: swirl the last of the bottle and pour the yeast in.

Looking is only the first step. The real skill is connecting what you see with what you smell and taste: haze with a sour note, a brown tint with cardboard. That connection comes with structured tasting practice. It is what separates a confident drinker from a guessing one.
Clarity is not a quality score

For decades many drinkers equated clear with clean and cloudy with cheap. The hazy IPA turned that round. Now some people assume haze means fresh and flavourful. Neither rule holds.

A clear beer can be stale. A hazy one can be brilliant. What matters is whether the appearance fits the style and the flavour backs it up.
faqs: No. Many styles are meant to be hazy, including hefeweizen, witbier and New England IPA. Haze is a problem only when it does not belong in the style or comes with off flavours.
Protein and polyphenol particles that form when beer is very cold and dissolve as it warms. It changes the look, not the taste.
Why are some beers so clear?
Time and cold let yeast and protein settle. Brewers also use finings or filtration to get a brilliant, clear beer.
Can haze mean a beer is infected?
Sometimes. Haze that does not clear, along with sour, vinegar or other odd flavours in a style that should not have them, can point to infection.
